verses.text: Again Yahweh’s anger burned against Israel, and he moved David against them, saying, “Go, count Israel and Judah.”

The king said to Joab the captain of the army, who was with him, “Now go back and forth through all the tribes of Israel, from Dan even to Beersheba, and count the people, that I may know the sum of the people.”

Joab said to the king, “Now may Yahweh your God add to the people, however many they may be, one hundred times; and may the eyes of my lord the king see it. But why does my lord the king delight in this thing?”
Notwithstanding, the king’s word prevailed against Joab, and against the captains of the army. Joab and the captains of the army went out from the presence of the king to count the people of Israel.
They passed over the Jordan, and encamped in Aroer, on the right side of the city that is in the middle of the valley of Gad, and to Jazer;
then they came to Gilead, and to the land of Tahtim Hodshi; and they came to Dan Jaan, and around to Sidon,
and came to the stronghold of Tyre, and to all the cities of the Hivites, and of the Canaanites; and they went out to the south of Judah, at Beersheba.
So when they had gone back and forth through all the land, they came to Jerusalem at the end of nine months and twenty days.
Joab gave up the sum of the counting of the people to the king: and there were in Israel eight hundred thousand valiant men who drew the sword; and the men of Judah were five hundred thousand men.

David’s heart struck him after he had counted the people. David said to Yahweh, “I have sinned greatly in that which I have done. But now, Yahweh, put away, I beg you, the iniquity of your servant; for I have done very foolishly.”
When David rose up in the morning, Yahweh’s word came to the prophet Gad, David’s seer, saying,
“Go and speak to David, ‘Yahweh says, “I offer you three things. Choose one of them, that I may do it to you.”’”

So Gad came to David, and told him, and said to him, “Shall seven years of famine come to you in your land? Or will you flee three months before your foes while they pursue you? Or shall there be three days’ pestilence in your land? Now answer, and consider what answer I shall return to him who sent me.”
David said to Gad, “I am in distress. Let us fall now into Yahweh’s hand; for his mercies are great. Let me not fall into man’s hand.”
So Yahweh sent a pestilence on Israel from the morning even to the appointed time; and seventy thousand men died of the people from Dan even to Beersheba.

When the angel stretched out his hand toward Jerusalem to destroy it, Yahweh relented of the disaster, and said to the angel who destroyed the people, “It is enough. Now withdraw your hand.” Yahweh’s angel was by the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.

David spoke to Yahweh when he saw the angel who struck the people, and said, “Behold, I have sinned, and I have done perversely; but these sheep, what have they done? Please let your hand be against me, and against my father’s house.”
Gad came that day to David, and said to him, “Go up, build an altar to Yahweh on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.”
David went up according to the saying of Gad, as Yahweh commanded.
Araunah looked out, and saw the king and his servants coming on toward him. Then Araunah went out, and bowed himself before the king with his face to the ground.
Araunah said, “Why has my lord the king come to his servant?” David said, “To buy your threshing floor, to build an altar to Yahweh, that the plague may be stopped from afflicting the people.”
Araunah said to David, “Let my lord the king take and offer up what seems good to him. Behold, the cattle for the burnt offering, and the threshing instruments and the yokes of the oxen for the wood.
All this, O king, does Araunah give to the king.” Araunah said to the king, “May Yahweh your God accept you.”

The king said to Araunah, “No; but I will most certainly buy it from you for a price. I will not offer burnt offerings to Yahweh my God which cost me nothing.” So David bought the threshing floor and the oxen for fifty shekels  of silver.
David built an altar to Yahweh there, and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings. So Yahweh was entreated for the land, and the plague was removed from Israel.

footnotes.content: Sometimes the Lord permits a king's pride to flourish so we see its full cost. David will count his strength as though it rests on numbers rather than on God's faithfulness. The anger that smolders here is love that will not let us settle for less than His truth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: From Dan to Beersheba—the whole nation, end to end. David gives the order with the certainty of a man who no longer sees his people as God's flock, but as his own possession to measure and manage. How often do we slip into counting what we ought to hold lightly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joab sees the danger before the king does. His protest is not mere flattery—he's asking aloud the question David should have asked himself: *Why do you want this?* A faithful counselor speaks into the spaces where pride is blind. Joab knows counting people is the work of men who've forgotten who owns the kingdom.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king's word overrides wisdom. Joab obeys, yet we see that even his obedience carries the weight of unease. Sometimes the hardest faithfulness is to follow orders we know are wrong—and live with that knowledge.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Aroer, Gad, Jazer—real places, real people touched by this useless mission. The census carries David's ambition across the land like a shadow, and ordinary lives feel its weight.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The men march through Gilead toward Dan, measuring, counting. Each town a stamp, each family a number. Can you hear the weariness in this survey? Joab moves swiftly, as though speed might shield him from the wrongness he feels.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All the way to Sidon, to Tyre—the edges of Israel's reach. The kingdom looks vast when you count it. And that is precisely the temptation: to believe your eyes instead of God's word.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Nine months and twenty days of counting. The work is done, thorough and complete. Now comes the moment of reckoning—when the numbers are laid before the king and his heart might finally ask why.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Eight hundred thousand in Israel, five hundred thousand in Judah. The sum is vast and empty. David wanted to know his strength, but numbers never tell you what your heart truly needs to know—that you are held by grace, not by the size of your army.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David's conscience strikes him like a blow. His heart *smites* him—there's violence in that word, and grace underneath it. He names his sin at once: pride, foolishness. The turning comes the moment he stops defending himself and sees what he's done.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gad the seer—David's prophet and friend—rises early to hear God's word. The Lord is already moving toward the king before dawn breaks, ready to offer him a path through the consequences he's invited. This is mercy before confession is even fully formed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three choices laid before the king: famine, flight, or pestilence. No escape, only different paths through pain. God offers the king something harder than forgiveness without cost—the chance to choose which consequence he will bear. This is grace that asks something of us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seven years of hunger. Three months hunted by enemies. Three days of sickness and death. Each choice cuts differently. Gad speaks plainly, inviting David to *consider*—to think through not just the facts, but what his choice says about who he trusts.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Let us fall into Yahweh's hand." David chooses the pestilence—swift and beyond human agency. He knows God's mercies are great; he fears far more the judgment of men. In this moment, his faith shows: he will take suffering from the hand of the Lord rather than cruelty from human enemies.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: From morning to the appointed time—death moves swiftly across the land. Seventy thousand men fall. The weight of David's choice rests on shoulders other than his own, and he sees it. This is the hardest part of repentance: living with the cost your sin carries for others.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The angel stretches his hand toward Jerusalem to finish his work, and the Lord says, "It is enough." Just there—at Araunah's threshing floor—judgment stops. The Lord has mercy on the city, and on David. The blow falls heavy but the sword does not fall on the whole kingdom.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I have sinned, but these sheep—what have they done?" David intercedes for his people with the rawness of a shepherd who sees them scattered by his own hand. He asks that the judgment stop with him, not with the innocent. This is a king finally thinking like a father.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gad returns with instruction: go to the threshing floor of Araunah and build an altar. The Lord names the exact place. Judgment and mercy meet on Araunah's ground—a place of harvest work that will become the place of atonement and the future site of the temple itself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David goes at once. No delay, no hesitation. He has learned that obedience after repentance is the language the Lord understands. The king moves quickly to do what the prophet speaks, and in that swift obedience he walks toward mercy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Araunah sees the king approaching with his servants. What does a Jebusite landowner feel at the sight of David? He bows low—respect, perhaps caution. The people sense when their king draws near, and he bows before a man who carries both authority and, now, the marks of humility.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "To buy your threshing floor, that the plague may be stopped." David explains his need plainly. He doesn't hide behind authority; he states what he wants and why. A threshing floor is nothing until it's made an altar—but on this ground, worship will turn away the Lord's judgment and begin to draw a broken kingdom toward healing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Araunah offers everything—cattle, instruments, wood. The landowner sees what David intends and opens his hands. He's willing to give his own livelihood for the king's altar. Sometimes a stranger's generosity teaches us more about grace than we expect.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "All this does Araunah give to the king." A gift offered freely. The Jebusite speaks a blessing: "May Yahweh your God accept you." He sees a man undone by his own pride, working to make it right, and he wishes him well. This is grace recognizing grace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David refuses to take the land or the cattle for nothing. "I will not offer to Yahweh which costs me nothing." He buys at full price—fifty shekels of silver—because worship born from repentance requires our own hand to give something real. When we come empty, we have nothing to lay down.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David builds his altar and offers the burnt offerings and peace offerings. The Lord hears and turns aside His anger. Readers today hear an echo in this story: a king who counted wrong things, saw his sin, and moved toward making it right—not perfectly, but truly. And the threshing floor becomes holy ground.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
